title: BFS queue scaffold
description: The canonical breadth-first search shell — queue + seen set, plus the level-snapshot variant for level-order traversal.

conversation.intro: How an interview about the BFS template would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before reaching for BFS — pin down the inputs and the answer shape.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given a graph and a start node, and I need to walk every reachable node in breadth-first order. Quick checks before I code:"

• How is the graph represented — adjacency list (object/map), adjacency matrix, or edge list? Adjacency list is what my template assumes.
• Is the graph directed or undirected? Affects whether I traverse `graph[cur]` once or both directions (the undirected case is usually pre-encoded in the adjacency list).
• Can a node have itself as a neighbor, or duplicate edges? The `seen` set handles both, but worth confirming.
• What do I return — visit order, just a count, or per-level groups? Variant A gives a flat order; Variant B groups by level.
sections.why: The 'adjacency list vs matrix' question changes the inner loop — `graph[cur]` vs `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (matrix[cur][i])`. Asking about per-level vs flat output is the move that lets you pick Variant A vs Variant B BEFORE writing code, so you don't have to refactor mid-implementation.

sections.title: 2. Why this template?
sections.prompt: What makes BFS the right tool over DFS here?
sections.say:
"BFS is the right tool when ORDER matters — specifically when you need shortest path in an unweighted graph, or per-level groupings. The reason: BFS expands by distance from the start, so the first time you reach any node is via a minimum-edge path. DFS doesn't give you that guarantee — it can find the target via a long detour first."

"The template has three load-bearing pieces:"

• `q = [start]` and `seen = new Set([start])` — initialize together so the start is never re-enqueued.
• `while (q.length)` + `q.shift()` — FIFO drain.
• Mark `seen.add(n)` BEFORE `q.push(n)` — the load-bearing ordering.
sections.why: Naming WHY BFS gives shortest path (distance-ordered expansion) distinguishes derivation from rote use. Most candidates can spell out the template; fewer can defend why it works. The 'mark before enqueue' ordering is the canonical interview trap — see section 3.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — mark-before-enqueue
sections.prompt: Why mark `seen` BEFORE pushing to the queue, not when you pop?
sections.say:
"This is the canonical BFS bug to inoculate against. If you wait until you dequeue to mark seen, then a high-degree node can be enqueued multiple times before any of those copies actually get popped — each of its predecessors sees it as 'unseen' and pushes a duplicate."

"Concrete example: graph A→C, B→C, A→B. From A: enqueue A; pop A, push B and C (mark A). Pop B (mark B), push C — but C was already in the queue! Without mark-before-enqueue, C is in the queue twice and gets visited twice. With mark-before-enqueue, when A pushes C it ALSO marks C, so B's loop sees `seen.has(C)` is true and skips."

"Same reasoning: never drop the `seen` set on a cyclic graph — you'd get an effectively infinite queue."
sections.why: This is the question I'd expect the interviewer to ask explicitly: 'why mark before push?' Having a concrete two-line example ready — not just 'to avoid duplicates' — is the senior-tier answer. The cyclic-graph extension (drop the seen set → infinite loop) is the second-order proof that the seen set is what makes BFS terminate on cycles.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: Three cases — the L3 prompt input (diamond shape with one shared sink), a linear chain (worst case for the queue length), and a single isolated node (degenerate case proving termination).

examples.note: Diamond — D is reachable from both B and C. The seen set prevents D from being enqueued twice.
examples.trace:
Init: q=['A'], seen={A}, order=[]
shift A → order=[A]. Neighbors B,C: B unseen → seen={A,B}, q=[B]. C unseen → seen={A,B,C}, q=[B,C]
shift B → order=[A,B]. Neighbors D: D unseen → seen={A,B,C,D}, q=[C,D]
shift C → order=[A,B,C]. Neighbors D: seen has D → skip. q=[D]
shift D → order=[A,B,C,D]. Neighbors=[]. q=[]
q empty → return [A,B,C,D] ✓
(Notice: C tried to enqueue D but seen.has(D) was already true.)

examples.note: Linear chain — queue holds at most one node at a time.
Single isolated node — proves the loop terminates on a graph of size 1.
examples.trace:
Init: q=[X], seen={X}, order=[]
shift X → order=[X]. Neighbors=[]. q=[]
return [X] ✓

sections.why: The diamond example is the load-bearing one — it's where 'mark-before-enqueue' earns its keep. Narrating 'C tried to enqueue D but seen.has(D) was already true' shows you traced the bug-vs-fix in your head. The linear-chain case demonstrates the queue stays small (BFS doesn't always have a fat queue), and the single-node case proves termination on the degenerate input.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs or coding choices would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges and pitfalls worth flagging:"

• Disconnected graphs → BFS only visits the start's connected component. If you need all nodes, wrap in an outer loop over unvisited starts.
• Cycles → handled by the `seen` set; drop the set and you get an infinite queue.
• `graph[cur]` undefined (a node with no entry, vs an entry with empty array) → `graph[cur] || []` guards against undefined.
• Forgot to mark start in `seen` → start might re-enqueue itself if a neighbor points back to it. Initialize `seen` with `new Set([start])`.
• Used `q.pop()` instead of `q.shift()` → silently turns into DFS. Same output sometimes; wrong on level-order or shortest-path problems.
• Huge graphs → `shift` is O(n); for millions of nodes use a head pointer or deque.
sections.why: The 'pop vs shift silently becomes DFS' point is the trap that catches careless candidates — the code still runs, sometimes returns the right answer, but is semantically wrong. The `graph[cur] || []` guard is the defensive touch for adjacency maps that may not have every node as a key. Naming the disconnected-graph case shows you've thought about whether BFS is a one-shot or needs to be looped.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(V + E) — each vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (V), and each edge is examined at most twice in an undirected adjacency representation, once in a directed one (E). The `seen` set's `has` and `add` are O(1) amortized.

The wrinkle: `q.shift()` is O(n) on a JS array, so the naive total is O(V·shift) = O(V²). For interview-scale (V≤10⁴) that's fine. For production, swap to a head-pointer to restore the textbook O(V + E).

Space is O(V) — the queue and seen set can each hold every vertex in the worst case.

The template generalizes hard. Variant B (level-order) adds one line — `const n = q.length` snapshot before the inner loop — and unlocks shortest-path-in-unweighted-graphs, binary-tree level traversal, and minimum-number-of-steps puzzles. Multi-source BFS (start with multiple nodes seeded into the queue) is the next layer up — that's how problems like 'rotting oranges' or 'walls and gates' are solved."
sections.why: The 'O(V·shift) = O(V²) for the naive form' admission is the senior-tier defense — interviewers want to hear you've thought about the constant factor, not just the asymptotic. Mentioning multi-source BFS unprompted is the transfer move that proves you see this as a template family, not a one-off.

walkthrough.intro: Step through Variant A (`bfsOrder`) — the queue + seen-set BFS template. Watch how mark-before-enqueue prevents the diamond's shared sink from being enqueued twice. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.
trace: yield { line: 3, label: `enter — start='${start}'`, state: { start, graph: JSON.stringify(graph) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `init — q=[${start}], seen={${start}}, order=[]`, state: { q: [...q], seen: [...seen], order: [...order] } };
yield { line: 8, label: `shift '${cur}' → order=${JSON.stringify(order)}, q=${JSON.stringify(q)}`, state: { cur, q: [...q], seen: [...seen], order: [...order] } };

yield { line: 13, label: `neighbor '${n}' unseen → mark and enqueue. seen={${[...seen].join(',')}}, q=${JSON.stringify(q)}`, state: { cur, neighbor: n, q: [...q], seen: [...seen], order: [...order] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `neighbor '${n}' already in seen → skip`, state: { cur, neighbor: n, q: [...q], seen: [...seen], order: [...order] } };
yield { line: 17, label: `q empty — return ${JSON.stringify(order)}`, state: { q: [...q], seen: [...seen], order: [...order], returns: JSON.stringify(order) } };

notes: Mark `seen` BEFORE enqueue, not after dequeue — otherwise a node can be enqueued multiple times before its first visit.
Array.shift is O(n); fine for interview-scale, but for huge queues use a head pointer or a real deque.
Level-order needs `const n = q.length` snapshotted BEFORE the inner loop — children pushed inside belong to the NEXT level.
Queue gives FIFO ⇒ BFS. Swap shift→pop and you've accidentally written DFS.

alternates.label: Multi-source BFS
alternates.when: Reach for this when the problem has MULTIPLE simultaneous starting points and asks for the minimum distance (or time) to reach every other node — Rotting Oranges, Walls and Gates, 01-Matrix. The trick: seed the queue with ALL sources at once, marked seen up-front. They expand in lock-step, so the first time any source reaches a node IS the shortest distance from the NEAREST source. Running single-source BFS from each start separately would be O(S·(V+E)); the multi-source version is one pass at O(V+E) regardless of how many sources you have.
notes: Seeding ALL sources at distance 0 up-front is the whole trick — they expand in lock-step, so the first arrival at any node comes from the NEAREST source. Running BFS from each source separately would be S× more work.
Same mark-before-enqueue discipline applies — without it a node mid-way between two sources gets enqueued twice and the distances may overwrite each other.
Returning a `dist` map gives you the shortest-distance-from-nearest-source for free in the same pass — no separate level-counting needed.

questions.q: What ordering does a BFS queue produce, and what data-structure operation gives it?
options: LIFO — push + pop
FIFO — push + shift
Sorted — push + sort
Random — push + splice
questions.explain: BFS visits nodes in arrival order: enqueue at the back (push), dequeue from the front (shift).

questions.q: Why mark a node in `seen` BEFORE enqueueing it (instead of when you dequeue)?
options: So the BFS depth-counter increments only on the dequeue side, keeping levels aligned
Otherwise multiple neighbors can each enqueue the same node before any of them gets visited
It's faster to call seen.add during enqueue than during dequeue on V8
Otherwise the `seen` set grows past the graph's node count and breaks O(V) space
questions.explain: If you wait until pop to mark seen, a high-degree node can be pushed many times — blowing up the queue and re-doing work.

questions.q: In the level-order BFS, why snapshot `const n = q.length` BEFORE the inner for-loop?
options: So `seen.size` matches `q.length` at the level boundary
Because children pushed during the inner loop belong to the NEXT level, not the current one
To handle the case where `q.shift()` returns undefined on an empty queue
Because reading `.length` inside the loop creates a new iterator and breaks `for...of`
questions.explain: Reading q.length live would grow as you push children, mixing the current level with the next.

questions.q: What's the actual cost of `queue.shift()` on a JS array of length n, and why is it acceptable here?
options: O(1) — same as pop
O(log n) — the array is a tree internally
O(n) — every remaining element re-indexes; fine for interview-scale, swap to a head pointer if huge
O(n^2) — both shift and rebuild are linear
questions.explain: shift re-indexes every remaining element. At interview scale (≤10^4) it's fine; at production scale, use a head index or deque.

questions.q: You change `q.shift()` to `q.pop()` but leave everything else. What traversal do you get?
options: BFS but with each level visited right-to-left
DFS — popping the back makes the queue a LIFO stack
Reverse-BFS — the same node set in reverse arrival order
Topological order, since pop drains the most-recently-discovered branch first
questions.explain: pop() takes the most-recently-pushed node (LIFO), which dives deep before broad — that's depth-first search, not breadth-first.

questions.q: For finding the shortest path in an UNWEIGHTED graph, why is BFS the right tool over DFS?
options: DFS can revisit ancestors via recursion, inflating the path length
BFS reaches nodes in non-decreasing distance order, so the first time you reach the target is via a shortest path
DFS finds A path but never the shortest because its recursion stack drops backtracking info
BFS sorts neighbors by distance before visiting, which DFS skips
questions.explain: BFS expands by levels (distance from start), so a node's first discovery is along a minimum-edge path; DFS may find the target via a long path first.

questions.q: You drop the `seen` set entirely from BFS on a graph with cycles. What happens?
options: Each node is still visited once because the FIFO queue can't hold duplicates
Nodes get enqueued repeatedly, causing redundant work or an effectively infinite/exploding queue on cyclic graphs
The traversal silently terminates early when a back-edge is reached, missing nodes
Output order stays correct but time complexity degrades from O(V+E) to O(V·E)
questions.explain: Without a visited check, every path back to a node re-enqueues it; on a cycle the queue never drains and work blows up. The seen set is what makes graph BFS terminate.
